label: Model parallelism is always faster than data parallelism
description:
Model parallelism (tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, FSDP) and data parallelism solve different problems — they don't compete on raw throughput in most cases. The belief that 'model parallelism is the next level of scaling' often confuses *enabling* something with *speeding up* something.

**Data parallelism** replicates the model. Throughput per GPU is high (each GPU does a full forward + backward locally) but memory per GPU is also high (full model + grads + optimizer). Limit: model size that fits one GPU.

**Tensor parallelism** shards each layer across GPUs. Memory per GPU drops; per-layer all-reduces add comm cost. On NVLink with large layers, the all-reduce overhead is small enough that TP can match DP throughput. **On slow interconnect or small layers, TP is slower than DP.**

**Pipeline parallelism** shards layers across GPUs. Comm is light (point-to-point activation transfer) but pipeline bubbles waste compute. Net throughput is often *lower* than DP per GPU; PP exists to fit bigger models, not to speed up smaller ones.

**FSDP / ZeRO-3** shards weights/grads/optimizer. Per-step cost roughly 2× DP's all-reduce volume; throughput is competitive with DP when DP fits and FSDP isn't strictly needed.

The correct framing: pick the strategy that *fits* your model + memory budget. Among strategies that fit, pick the one with the highest throughput. Multi-strategy hybrids (TP intra-host + PP inter-host + DP across replicas) are common at frontier scale because no single strategy fits both the memory and throughput requirements.

The wrong move: applying TP/PP to a model that fits in DP. The added comm cost makes training slower without enabling anything new.
probeQuestions: If a model fits in DDP comfortably, would switching to TP make training faster?
When does pipeline parallelism become a throughput speedup vs a memory enabler?
correctionPromptTemplate: The learner thinks model parallelism is universally faster. Reframe: each parallelism strategy *enables* a different scale, and only some of them are also throughput improvements. DDP is the per-GPU throughput champion when the model fits. TP/PP/FSDP enable bigger models at the cost of comm overhead. The right strategy depends on what fits + what's bandwidth-available. Ask first — 'what's the constraint your current setup is hitting: memory, throughput, or training instability?'
